title: Singapore to step up surveillance of three infectious diseases from Oct 31

analysis.time: Singapore will step up surveillance of three infectious diseases starting from Oct 31, 2026, as per the article published on Oct 18, 2026. The CDA has been monitoring these diseases for some time, and the latest amendment to the Infectious Diseases Act (IDA) was made in September 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Singapore, with medical practitioners, clinical laboratories, and the general population being affected. The surveillance includes all confirmed and suspected cases of the three diseases.
analysis.event: Singapore has increased surveillance of three infectious diseases—Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever, Lassa fever, and Marburg virus disease—by adding them to the IDA list. This is a policy change to enhance preparedness and response capabilities.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The three diseases have high fatality rates, up to 50% for Marburg virus disease, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). However, the risk to Singapore remains low. The CDA will monitor and report on these diseases weekly starting in November 2026.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDA is enhancing surveillance and preparedness efforts, including early detection, isolation of cases, and contact tracing. The WHO notes there is no specific treatment or vaccine for these diseases, though research is ongoing. The risk level remains low, and the surveillance measures are designed to ensure readiness.

analysis.brief_en: Singapore has announced plans to enhance surveillance of three infectious diseases—Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever, Lassa fever, and Marburg virus disease—starting from October 31, 2026. This decision follows amendments to the Infectious Diseases Act (IDA) in September 2026, which added these diseases to the list of monitored pathogens. The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that these diseases have high fatality rates, up to 50% for Marburg virus disease, but the risk to Singapore remains low. The Communicable Diseases Agency (CDA) emphasized that the changes aim to strengthen the nation's preparedness and response capabilities. Medical practitioners and clinical laboratories are now legally required to report all confirmed and suspected cases. The CDA will include these diseases in its weekly bulletin starting in November 2026, ensuring ongoing monitoring and timely public health actions. No specific treatments or vaccines are currently available, though research is ongoing for Lassa fever and Marburg virus disease.
analysis.summary_en: Singapore has announced plans to enhance surveillance of three infectious diseases—Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever, Lassa fever, and Marburg virus disease—starting from October 31, 2026. This decision follows amendments to the Infectious Diseases Act (IDA) in September 2026, which added these diseases to the list of monitored pathogens. The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that these diseases have high fatality rates, up to 50% for Marburg virus disease, but the risk to Singapore remains low. The Communicable Diseases Agency (CDA) emphasized that the changes aim to strengthen the nation's preparedness and response capabilities. Medical practitioners and clinical laboratories are now legally required to report all confirmed and suspected cases. The CDA will include these diseases in its weekly bulletin starting in November 2026, ensuring ongoing monitoring and timely public health actions. No specific treatments or vaccines are currently available, though research is ongoing for Lassa fever and Marburg virus disease.

title: UK Commits £33.2 Million to Eight Vaccine Projects Targeting Ebola, Marburg, Plague and Other Epidemic Threats - Global Biodefense

analysis.time: The UK government announced the funding on October 8, 2026, with the news published on October 18, 2026. The funding is intended to advance vaccine development for diseases with epidemic potential.
analysis.location_and_population: The funding is targeted at low- and middle-income countries, with a focus on diseases that pose significant threats globally, including those affecting humans and animals.
analysis.event: The UK government committed £33.2 million to eight vaccine projects targeting Marburg virus and other epidemic threats, as stated by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) and Innovate UK.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The funding aims to build research, clinical trial, and technical capacity to develop, test, and deploy vaccines quickly for emerging threats, ensuring affordability and accessibility in high-risk countries.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The funding is part of the UK Vaccine Network, which is designed to address market failures in vaccine development for deadly diseases. The response includes advancing vaccine candidates and technologies for novel pathogens.

analysis.brief_en: The UK government has committed £33.2 million to eight vaccine projects targeting Marburg virus and other epidemic threats, as announced by the Department of Health and Social Care, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), and Innovate UK on October 8, 2026. The funding aims to accelerate vaccine development and deployment for diseases with epidemic potential, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. This initiative is part of the UK Vaccine Network, which addresses market failures by supporting research, clinical trials, and technologies for emerging pathogens. The UK has previously invested £134 million in its first phase between 2016 and 2022, with further funding planned for 2023 to 2029. The program also includes efforts to develop vaccines for other diseases such as Ebola, plague, Lassa fever, Nipah virus, chikungunya, and Mayaro virus. Richard Pebody, UKHSA’s Director of Epidemic and Emerging Infections, emphasized the importance of preparedness, citing the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and a suspected pneumonic plague case in Russia as reminders of persistent infectious disease risks. The funding will not support pathogens with existing licensed vaccines or advanced candidates, nor SARS-CoV-2 or influenza.
analysis.summary_en: The UK government has committed £33.2 million to eight vaccine projects targeting Marburg virus and other epidemic threats, as announced by the Department of Health and Social Care, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), and Innovate UK on October 8, 2026. The funding aims to accelerate vaccine development and deployment for diseases with epidemic potential, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. This initiative is part of the UK Vaccine Network, which addresses market failures by supporting research, clinical trials, and technologies for emerging pathogens. The UK has previously invested £134 million in its first phase between 2016 and 2022, with further funding planned for 2023 to 2029. The program also includes efforts to develop vaccines for other diseases such as Ebola, plague, Lassa fever, Nipah virus, chikungunya, and Mayaro virus. Richard Pebody, UKHSA’s Director of Epidemic and Emerging Infections, emphasized the importance of preparedness, citing the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and a suspected pneumonic plague case in Russia as reminders of persistent infectious disease risks. The funding will not support pathogens with existing licensed vaccines or advanced candidates, nor SARS-CoV-2 or influenza.
